717.t: Pricing arrangements and doing work for love
717.s: Abene advises using Local 802 orchestrator scale as a gauge for pricing, and describes taking jobs like Mel Lewis's band for the music.
717.q: The skeleton of it all, and then you give it to the orchestrator, and some of these orchestrators you never heard of, who are not only fabulous but that’s also a very lucrative — the only bad part for me would be it’s like being buried under something else you know. So I was never inclined to do…

718.s: He has a standard fee, negotiates, and prices exclusives differently.
718.q: I have a kind of a standard fee and then I tell the group look — especially if it’s a group that’s a professional or a highly touted university group, if it’s something that I really don’t have a lot of limitations to then I’ll work with you. If you can’t afford my price, let

719.t: Producers' reactions to his parts and getting paid
719.s: Producers hire him for what he has done before; he will change anything and has rarely gone unpaid.
719.q: Well I don’t know if they, you know, really Quincy may, Foster may, but you know a lot of the other people that are more producers and less musician, you know they’re not necessarily, but the reason they hired me was because they liked what I’ve done in the past, so they know, I guess they’re…

720.s: Price depends on the client and what he can get.
720.q: Well it depends on who you’re working for, for one thing. If it’s a pop act that’s one thing, if it’s a jazz guy it’s another thing. If it’s a record company paying for it that’s another thing. So there are several different things that go into it, plus your own price, you know what you’re able to…

721.s: Malone describes the union per-bar formula used for Shaffer and the checks for Renee Fleming and Atlantic.
721.q: Oh well there’s a formula — the union book has a way — it’s by the measure or the score page or something. There’s a way of breaking it down. So it’s all mathematical.

617.t: Pricing his compositions and playing the same for any audience
617.s: He is unsure how to price writing, uses a sliding scale, and says he plays the same for ten or ten thousand, citing Milt Hinton and Slide Hampton.
617.q: That is difficult. Because like I say, I am a novice so I really feel I can’t do it. Because I’m slow. It takes me time. Although if they give me a timeline, that helps. Because now I say well this is a chunk of time in order for me to do this. I ask some friends, and I look

722.s: He has no set fee, asks about budgets, and sometimes works free or as a guest artist package.
722.q: Not specifically. The way that I’ve always kind of done it is most of the time if I get called it’s not really blind calls, it’s somebody that either I was in school with or maybe played in my band or somebody that I know. And so the way that I’ve always worked that is I do the best I can to find…

487.t: Pricing arrangements and sharing rates with other arrangers
487.s: Union minimums, quoting prices, record companies balking then paying later, and telling fellow arrangers about a higher rate.
487.q: Yes. There is a minimum scale and as time went by and I started getting more recognition, and to be honest the work I was doing — better work — I was more pleased with what I was doing. It got to a point where now when someone calls about an arrangement I’ll ask about the instrumentation, get as…

613.t: What to charge and knowing your worth
613.s: He does not know others' rates, negotiates occasionally, and says giving work away cheaply lowers respect, including for streaming.
613.q: I have no idea what other people charge. Maybe I don’t have the courage to ask them. And I figure if I ask them it’s kind of invading their privacy and then they don’t ask me because you know, if I gave out that information someone would try to undercut me of course, or vice versa.

166.t: Court, and whether he worked over or under scale
166.s: In court he stayed silent about pay; he insists he always asked over scale.
166.q: So I go to court and they read the charges and everything. Now I can't tell why we were fighting, otherwise I'm going to blow it on Sid and Ben and all three of us will get kicked out of the union. I can't open my mouth.
